title: Raja ne apna maans kaise kaata kabutar bachane?
hooks: Raja ne apna maans kaata... kabutar bachane ke liye
Ek Raja apni jaan tarazu pe rakh di... ek chhote kabutar ke liye
Baaz ne maang liya Raja ka maans... phir kya hua?
hook_why: Opens with the most shocking visual — a king cutting his own flesh — in the first 4 words. The pigeon gives an instant visual anchor. No greeting, no intro.
metaphor: Tarazu (weighing scale) — the scale is the visual backbone: each beat adds weight to one pan (king's flesh) vs the other (pigeon), showing compassion outweighing self-preservation.

cast.Raja Megharath: ancient Indian king, calm compassionate face, saffron dhoti with gold border, seated on marble throne in ornate Jain temple courtyard, gentle glow
cast.Kabutar: white pigeon, soft feathers, gentle dark eyes, small and vulnerable
cast.Baaz: fierce hawk, sharp hooked beak, piercing eyes, powerful wings, predator stance
cast.Mantri: elderly minister in white cotton dhoti-angvastra, folded hands, concerned expression
cast.Devta: two celestial beings in radiant white silk, golden ornaments, serene divine glow, floating above ground

caption:
Raja Megharath ne apna maans kaat diya ek kabutar bachane ke liye. Yehi karuna unhe 16ve Tirthankar Shantinath bana di. Srot: Adipurana.

Tum hote toh apna maans dete?

Jai Jinendra 🙏

claims.claim: King Megharath cut his own flesh to save a pigeon from a hawk
claims.basis: Adipurana / Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra (Hemachandra) — both jainknowledge.com and jainworld.com recount the identical episode

claims.claim: The pigeon and hawk were devas testing the king's compassion
claims.basis: Same sources: Indra sent two devas in pigeon and hawk form to test earthly kings

claims.claim: King refused butcher's meat to avoid indirect killing
claims.basis: Explicit in both sources: 'butcher may have to kill another animal'

claims.claim: King sat on the weighing scale himself when flesh was insufficient
claims.basis: Both sources: 'Finally the king was getting ready to put his whole body on the scale'

claims.claim: King Megharath's soul became the 16th Tirthankara Shantinath
claims.basis: Both sources conclude: 'Later on, the soul of King Meghrath became the sixteenth Tirthankar, Shantinath'
